title: Base change of finite coefficient formulas on unrestricted formal series
statement:
Let $R,S$ be commutative rings, $\sigma:R\to S$ a unital ring homomorphism, and $T=(T_1,\ldots,T_t)$ a finite set of formal variables [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Consider $R$-linear operators specified by finite expressions using addition, composition, multiplication by fixed full formal series, insertion of unused variables, partial coefficient extractions
$$E_{U,\beta}:R[[U,V]]\to R[[V]],\qquad E_{U,\beta}\Bigl(\sum_\eta a_\eta(V)U^\eta\Bigr)=a_\beta(V),$$
where $(U,V)$ partitions the variables, and multiplication by finite matrices over $R$ or their specified inverses [def-weil-matrix]. Every expression has matching source and target variable sets. Let $P:R[[T]]\to R[[T]]$ be such an expression. Applying $\sigma$ to every scalar coefficient and every full series defines an $S$-linear operator $P_\sigma:S[[T]]\to S[[T]]$, with
$$P_\sigma\,\sigma_*H=\sigma_*PH,\qquad \sigma_*\Bigl(\sum_\nu a_\nu T^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_\nu\sigma(a_\nu)T^\nu.$$
Each output coefficient depends on finitely many input coefficients. The operators are continuous for the topology in which coefficients are discrete and a net converges when each coefficient is eventually fixed. All equalities between such operator expressions, and all equalities of their values on specified series, persist under $\sigma$; matrices and their specified inverses still multiply to the identity. In particular, if $P$ is a projection onto the common kernel of any given family of partial coefficient tests $E_{U,\beta}$ (its image is contained in that kernel and it fixes every member of the kernel), then $P_\sigma$ is a projection onto the common kernel of the same tests on $S[[T]]$. Tests here vanish as full series in the complementary variables.
In addition suppose that $S$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. If $f_1,\ldots,f_q\in R[[T]]$ and
$$(P-1)(R[[T]])\subseteq(f_1,\ldots,f_q),$$
then, for unrestricted inputs,
$$(P_\sigma-1)(S[[T]])\subseteq(\sigma_*f_1,\ldots,\sigma_*f_q).$$
This applies in particular when $L$ is a field [def-weil-field], $X$ a finite variable set and $\tau:R\to L[[X]]$ any unital ring homomorphism: the ring $L[[X]]$ is Noetherian and, identifying $L[[X]][[T]]=L[[X,T]]$ by coefficient families, $(P_\tau-1)(L[[X,T]])\subseteq(\tau_*f_1,\ldots,\tau_*f_q)$. All the constructions commute with composition of coefficient homomorphisms. In particular they commute with continuous changes of the coefficient variables $X$ that fix $T$. Empty variable sets, empty matrices, zero generators, and zero tests are allowed.

proof.text: For two equal operator expressions $A=B$, evaluate on each monomial $T^\nu$ with coefficient $1$: their $(\mu,\nu)$ entries agree in $R$. Applying $\sigma$ to these entries and using the finite row formulas proves $A_\sigma=B_\sigma$ on all $S$-series, without any surjectivity of $\sigma$. An equality of values on specified series is transported by the intertwining identity of Step 2. Matrix inverse identities are finite entrywise identities $\sum_j M_{ij}N_{jk}=\delta_{ik}$ and $\sum_j N_{ij}M_{jk}=\delta_{ik}$, so they persist as well. No inverse of a new matrix is chosen.

proof.text:
Let $D$ be the union of the input multi-indices selected by the given partial coefficient tests, including every index in their complementary variables. Their common kernel consists exactly of series whose coefficients on $D$ vanish. For $\mu\in D$, the hypothesis that the image of $P$ lies in that kernel, evaluated on every $T^
u$, says $a_{\mu
u}=0$ for all $
u$. For $
u
otin D$, the monomial $T^
u$ belongs to the kernel, so the fixing hypothesis says $a_{\mu
u}=\delta_{\mu
u}$ for every $\mu$. These entry identities persist under $\sigma$. The first identities give the image condition over $S$; the second, inserted in the finite row formula for an arbitrary series supported off $D$, give $P_\sigma H'=H'$. Hence it is the required projection (and is idempotent). This argument allows an infinite family of tests.

proof.text: For any coefficient ring $S$, put $B=S[[T]]$ and $I=(T_1,\ldots,T_t)$. A series belongs to $I^n$ exactly when its coefficients of total degree less than $n$ vanish: one implication follows by convolution; for the other assign each monomial of degree at least $n$ to one of its finitely many degree-$n$ divisors and collect the corresponding quotient series. Thus coefficientwise convergence and $I$-adic convergence agree when $T$ is finite. Also $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical: for $h\in I$ and $b\in B$, the series $\sum_{r\geq0}(bh)^r$ is well defined coefficient by coefficient and is an inverse of $1-bh$ by telescoping. If $h$ were outside some maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, choose $b$ inverse to its nonzero residue in $B/\mathfrak m$; then the unit $1-bh$ would lie in $\mathfrak m$, a contradiction.

source.place: Agent coefficient-family argument for the operator assertion; Tags 0306 (lemma-Noetherian-power-series) and 00IQ (lemma-intersection-powers-ideal-module), part (2), for the ideal assertion.

proof.text: Now assume $S$ Noetherian. By [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-noetherian], $B=S[[T]]$ is Noetherian. For every ideal $J\subseteq B$, the quotient $M=B/J$ is a finite $B$-module, generated by $1+J$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-krull-intersection-jacobson] to $B,I,M$, with the Jacobson containment from Step 5, obtaining $\bigcap_n I^nM=0$. Since $I^nM=(I^n+J)/J$, this is $\bigcap_n(J+I^n)=J$. Thus a coefficientwise limit of elements of $J$ belongs to $J$: modulo each $I^n$ it eventually agrees with such an element by Step 5. This establishes precisely the closedness needed here, without assuming that $S$ is local or that $R\to S$ is flat.

proof.text: Every ideal of a field $L$ is either zero or contains a nonzero element and hence $1$, so $L$ is Noetherian by [def-weil-field, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-noetherian] with the finite variable set $X$ to get that $S=L[[X]]$ is Noetherian, and apply Step 7 to $\tau$. Regrouping coefficients via $\mathbf N^X\times\mathbf N^T=\mathbf N^{X\sqcup T}$ identifies $L[[X]][[T]]$ with $L[[X,T]]$ as rings: both products sum over the same finite decompositions of each pair of exponents. This is an identification of coefficient families; no equality of differently chosen topologies is needed. For $R\xrightarrow{\sigma}S\xrightarrow{\rho}A$, every transported row entry is $\rho(\sigma(a_{\mu\nu}))$, equal to the entry transported along $\rho\sigma$. The same coefficient equality applies to each specified series and matrix. This proves compatibility with composition, including continuous changes of the coefficient variables $X$ fixing $T$. If $T$ is empty there is one index, $I=0$, and truncations are already the entire input for $N\geq1$; empty tuples and matrices give empty sums, zero generators give $J=0$, and no tests give $D=\varnothing$ and force $P=1$.
